explicit_definitions_given: Confession as personal declaration of allegiance
Narration as placement within salvation history
World as an order of pride and domination

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Implicitly addresses objections by distinguishing martyrdom from proof and by emphasizing the Holy Ghost as mediator.
objections_raised: Martyrdom does not automatically prove truth
Personal testimony risks becoming empty interiority
Historical narration risks becoming detached tradition

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Conceptual analysis and scriptural narrative interpretation

philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Testimony, witness, juridical accountability, salvation history

summary_of_core_decisions: The text defines testimony as a boundary phenomenon irreducible to either subjective feeling or objective information. It uses Ricoeur's semantic/juridical analysis to establish the structure, then applies it to LDS theology and the Abinadi narrative. The central dialectic is between testimony-confession (personal self-involvement) and testimony-narration (historical content), resolved by the Holy Ghost as mediator. Abinadi's trial dramatizes the accused/emissary paradox, martyrdom as reversal, and the cosmic struggle between Christ and the world.
